Hi! In #37531 I computed the law of the docs#ProbabilityTheory.binomial distribution introduced in #28248. Then I used this to compute the expectation. But of course the nicer proof would be to use the fact that a sum of iid Bernoullis has a binomial distribution (and that would be even nicer for the variance). I know several people used a version in side projects, but I think in mathlib there is only PMF.bernoulli? From what I gathered the issue is that depending on context there are many different types on which one would like the measure to be defined.

Is there one idea that seems better than others to implement this? If so I am happy to try and proceed with this. I briefly thought about defining it for arbitrary points as:

import Mathlib

open MeasureTheory unitInterval

noncomputable def bernoulliMeasure {X : Type*} [MeasurableSpace X] (p : I) (x y : X) : Measure X :=
  toNNReal p • Measure.dirac x + toNNReal (σ p) • Measure.dirac y

but did not try to implement it so probably this comes with some issues.

Side question: apart from the expectation, #37531 is interesting on its own, but should I wait for the Bernoulli discussion to settle and then use it to compute the expectation more elegantly, or is it fine to use a direct computation? One could also argue that a more principled way would be: for each distribution in mathlib, compute the characteristic function first, then deduce moments.
I wrote essentially this definition in my draft at #35766 (Except I used toENNReal but now I believe to NNReal is better). Feel free to take whatever from that.
